findings.title: VSCode extension subtree is MIT-only with a different copyright holder than the dual-licensed root
findings.description: editors/vscode/LICENSE declares 'Copyright (c) 2026 Buff Lang Project' and MIT only, while the root project is dual 'MIT OR Apache-2.0' under 'Vinicius Schwinden Berkenbrock' (LICENSE-MIT:3, LICENSE-APACHE:189, README License section). editors/vscode/README.md License section claims 'MIT - same as the rest of the Buff toolchain', which is inaccurate: the toolchain is dual-licensed. Deviation from the declared AGENTS.md convention (license = MIT OR Apache-2.0).
findings.root_cause: Subtree license authored independently of the root dual-license setup; AGENTS.md inside the subtree self-declares 'License: MIT', entrenching the drift; README prose copied without reconciling with root licensing.
findings.impact: Ambiguous attribution for a shipped artifact (buff-vscode .vsix); consumers relying on the extension README cannot exercise the Apache-2.0 option available for the rest of the project; copyright-holder mismatch complicates provenance chains and future relicensing audits.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) align the subtree to the root: replace editors/vscode/LICENSE header with the root holder and add dual LICENSE files, updating package.json 'license' to 'MIT OR Apache-2.0' and the subtree AGENTS.md; or (b) keep MIT-only deliberately but fix the README sentence to state it is MIT-only, not 'same as the toolchain', and record the decision in .sisyphus/decisions/.

detection_method.query: Select-String Copyright across editors/vscode/LICENSE vs LICENSE-MIT

confidence.rationale: Both files read in full; holder strings differ verbatim; README claim contradicts root dual license; subtree AGENTS.md self-declares MIT, confirming intent drift.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Direct textual comparison of license headers; no inference required. Subtree is internally MIT-consistent, so this is attribution/consistency (medium), not missing-license (high).

findings.title: Global license confidence-threshold lowered to 0.6 to accommodate one legacy crate
findings.description: deny.toml [licenses] sets confidence-threshold = 0.6 (lines 147-150) explicitly to admit ring 0.16.20 (OpenSSL dual license, inference score 0.66). This is a workspace-wide loosening: any transitive crate whose license cargo-deny infers at >=0.6 confidence passes, even when the classifier is uncertain, not just ring. Allow-list itself is sound: no GPL/AGPL, no copyleft-strong entries, no skip/ignore entries in [licenses]; MPL-2.0/CDDL-1.0 (file-level copyleft) are compatible with MIT OR Apache-2.0 distribution.
findings.root_cause: Workaround for a single legacy pinned dependency (ring 0.16.20 pulled by ethers/jsonwebtoken) applied as a global knob instead of a scoped clarification.
findings.impact: Weakened license gate: a mis-inferred or ambiguously licensed new transitive dependency could silently pass CI where the default 0.8 threshold would flag it for review; no immediate incompatibility today (allow-list verified clean).
findings.recommendation: Restore the default threshold and add a scoped [licenses.clarifications] entry for ring 0.16.20 (license = 'OpenSSL OR ISC'), or bump the legacy ring consumer to 0.17 (score above threshold) and delete the override.

findings.fix_guide: 1) Set confidence-threshold back to 0.8. 2) Add a clarifications block scoped to ring 0.16.20. 3) Run cargo deny check licenses locally; clarify any other sub-0.8 crates individually rather than lowering globally.

confidence.rationale: Verified verbatim in deny.toml lines 147-150 with inline comment stating the single-crate motivation; risk is hygiene-level, not a current violation.

fp_risk_self_assessment.reasoning: Exact line evidence; the allow-list itself contains no GPL/AGPL and no [licenses] skip entries, so no compat finding was asserted beyond the threshold hygiene note.
